content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has released updated guidelines in April 2021 regarding the delivery of services for the treatment and care of individuals living with HIV. These guidelines are available in both electronic and print formats, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-002358-1 and 978-92-4-002359-8. The guidelines include a comprehensive table of contents, covering topics such as differentiated service delivery for HIV treatment, people-centered care, initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) outside health facilities, rapid ART initiation (including same-day start), clinical visit frequency, ART pick-up schedules, tracing and re-engagement in care, adherence assessment, integration of diabetes and hypertension care with HIV care, psychosocial interventions for adolescents and young adults living with HIV, task-sharing for specimen collection and point-of-care testing, diagnostic integration, and the dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of the guidelines. Key definitions are provided for terms such as advanced HIV disease, age groups (infants, children, adolescents, and adults), differentiated service delivery, integrated service delivery, people-centered care, key populations, rapid ART initiation, and vulnerable populations. For example, advanced HIV disease in adults, adolescents, and children aged five years or older is defined as a CD4 cell count of less than 200 cells/mm³ or the presence of a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event. All children under five years of age living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease. The guidelines promote a public health approach to HIV programming and service delivery, which has enabled the scaling up of treatment and care in resource-limited settings. The 2016 WHO consolidated guidelines on antiretroviral drug use included recommendations for delivering HIV services across the care cascade, from testing to long-term viral suppression. The 2021 update builds on this foundation, providing new recommendations and good practice statements in areas such as initiating ART, clinical visit frequency, adherence measurement, tracing and re-engagement, psychosocial support for adolescents, task-sharing for diagnostic services, and service integration. The guidelines were developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to evidence review and recommendation formulation. They are intended primarily for national HIV program managers and policymakers in lowand middle-income countries but are also a valuable resource for clinicians and other stakeholders involved in HIV care and policy development. Acknowledgments are given to numerous individuals and organizations who contributed to the development of these guidelines, including methodologists, members of the Service Delivery Guideline Development Group, external reviewers, evidence reviewers, WHO staff, consultants, and regional and country offices. Funding for the guidelines was provided by the United States President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), Unitaid, and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
